ops: West's heart opening lead is won by South.
South must avoid losing a trick to the @CJ in order to come to 12 tricks. The club combination is common and is frequently misplayed.
South should begin by leading a club towards dummy.
the @CK or @CQ should be played from dummy.
It is a well-known defensive tactic for East to duck with @CA doubleton of clubs in this situation in order to leave declarer with a guess on the second round. When the @CQ holds the first trick,
South has no inference as to the position of the @CA.
South returns to the closed hand
it seems that South has a strict guess.
Playing a low club will work when East began with doubleton @CA.
Playing the @CK will work when East began with a doubleton @CJ. The odds of these 2 holdings are the same.

This is actually not a guess. It is correct to play the @CK on the second round. When a declarer is faced with a problem such as this, he should formulate a plan and not deviate from that plan based on the defenders' early plays in the suit.
If declarer's plan is to play West for the @CJ on the second round of the suit,
it is irrelevant whether East wins the @CA on the first round when holding a doubleton. Declarer will always pick up that holding no matter how East defends.
If declarer's plan is to play West for the @CA on the second round of the suit,
East, holding doubleton @CA, can always defeat the contract by ducking the first round.
If East wins the @CA on the first round, South should play him for @CAJ doubleton.

The above club layout should only be picked up if declarer was planning on playing the @CK on the second round of the suit. This holding makes it correct to play the @CK on the second round regardless of whether East wins the @CA or the @CQ holds on the first round.
